content: Some of the most compelling evidence supporting tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) comes from the TEMPRANO trial conducted in Côte d’Ivoire. This study demonstrated that people living with HIV (PLHIV) who received isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) experienced a 37% reduction in mortality, regardless of whether they were also on antiretroviral therapy (ART). The greatest protection against severe disease and death was observed in individuals receiving both IPT and ART. Currently recommended TPT regimens provide long-lasting protection after a single course of treatment for PLHIV, HIV-negative individuals exposed to TB, and other at-risk populations. The protective effect of IPT has been shown to last between 6 and 19 years. Modern TPT regimens, which combine two TB drugs such as isoniazid and rifapentine or rifampicin, can be completed in just 3 to 4 months. These shorter regimens are as effective as older treatments in preventing TB disease progression and are easier for patients to complete. Although they may have higher short-term costs, they are more cost-effective overall because more individuals complete their prescribed treatment. Patients on shorter regimens are up to three times more likely to complete their course of TPT compared to those on longer regimens, leading to better outcomes and saving more lives. Education about the signs and symptoms of serious side effects, such as drug-induced hepatitis, is critical. Explaining the need for a weeksto months-long treatment course, even in the absence of illness, can be challenging. However, supporting patients to complete the full course of TPT is vital. There is no clear evidence to date that TPT increases TB drug resistance. However, it is essential to rule out active TB disease using recommended procedures before starting TPT. If screening is negative, the likelihood of active TB is minimal. Withholding TPT represents a missed opportunity to protect individuals and communities from preventable disease and death, which could be considered unethical. Concerns about harming otherwise healthy individuals should be addressed, as adverse events from TPT are rare, self-limiting, and reversible. Shorter rifamycin-based regimens have a better safety profile, and offering different options for various populations can help minimize risks. All individuals prescribed TPT should be clearly informed about the treatment schedule, potential side effects, and health alerts to watch for. They should be encouraged to contact their healthcare provider or stop TPT if serious adverse events occur. Systematic recording and reporting are essential for monitoring individual care and program performance. With appropriate training, nurses and frontline healthcare workers can manage most clinical duties related to TPT, reducing the need for specialist input except in complex cases. Key messages for PLHIV and individuals offered TPT include the following: You or your family members do not have active TB disease but may have a latent TB infection that could become active. TB is a serious disease that can threaten your life and spread to others. Your healthcare provider has determined that you would benefit from TPT, even if you are currently healthy. TPT can reduce your risk of developing TB by 60–90%. Most individuals on TPT experience no discomfort or side effects. If side effects occur, your caregiver will provide follow-up care to address them. Completing the full course of TPT as prescribed is essential for optimal protection. If you notice any adverse events, consult your healthcare provider immediately. For signs of serious issues, such as jaundice, stop TPT and seek care promptly. If you are on a rifamycin-based TPT regimen and wish to avoid pregnancy, note that rifapentine and other rifamycins reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives. Consider using alternative or barrier contraceptive methods. Parents or guardians should know that giving TPT to children protects them from TB, which can be difficult to diagnose and have long-term negative effects. Child-friendly medicines that dissolve in water and have a pleasant taste are now available, making it easier for children to adhere to treatment. For the community, it is important to understand that TB is a contagious disease transmitted through the air when an infected person coughs. Even with successful treatment, TB can cause lasting damage to the lungs or other organs, affecting quality of life. However, TB is preventable, and prevention is better than cure. Early detection and treatment of TB cases, BCG vaccination for infants, and TPT for at-risk individuals are effective strategies to reduce the burden of TB in the community. Community engagement and education are critical to increasing awareness and demand for TPT, particularly among high-risk groups such as PLHIV, children, and household contacts of TB patients.
